# Polycystic ovary syndrome

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Endocrinology > Disorders of glucose metabolism > Polycystic ovary syndrome*

[Original Article Link](/library/AO0RET)

---

## Summary

Polycystic <u>ovary</u> syndrome (PCOS) is one of the most common endocrine disorders in women. It is characterized by <u>hyperandrogenism</u> (which primarily manifests as <u>hirsutism</u>, <u>acne vulgaris</u>, and <u>androgenic alopecia</u>), <u>oligoovulation</u>/<u>anovulation</u>, and/or the presence of polycystic <u>ovaries</u>. The diagnosis involves a complete history and <u>physical examination</u> to evaluate for <u>ovulatory dysfunction</u> and clinical <u>signs of hyperandrogenism</u>. Laboratory tests are performed to confirm biochemical <u>hyperandrogenism</u> and exclude other conditions with a potentially similar clinical picture (e.g., <u>congenital adrenal hyperplasia</u>). <u>Ultrasound</u> may be performed in adults to identify cystic follicles and assess ovarian volume but is not required for diagnosis if <u>ovulatory dysfunction</u> and <u>hyperandrogenism</u> are present. Management consists of lifestyle modifications combined with specific treatment, which is tailored to the patient's reproductive goals. In women who do not wish to conceive, <u>combined oral contraceptive pills</u> are indicated to regulate <u>menses</u> and treat <u>hyperandrogenism</u>. For women who wish to conceive, the goal of treatment is to induce <u>ovulation</u> (e.g., with <u>letrozole</u>). Women with PCOS are twice as likely to develop <u>metabolic syndrome</u>, which is associated with <u>obesity</u>, <u>insulin resistance</u>, <u>hypercholesterolemia</u>, and an increased risk of <u>endometrial cancer</u>. Therefore, all patients should be screened for comorbidities and receive specific treatment for these when necessary.

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u>: 6–12% of women in their reproductive years in the US [[1]](/library/UfbblG)



Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Pathophysiology

* The exact pathophysiology is unknown.

* Strong association with <u>obesity</u> → ↑ in peripheral <u>estrogen</u> synthesis from <u>adipose tissue</u> and ↓ in peripheral <u>sensitivity</u> to <u>insulin</u>  [[2]](/library/b5XHiA)

* Reduced <u>insulin sensitivity</u> (<u>peripheral insulin resistance</u>) and the consequent <u>hyperinsulinemia</u> result in:

* <u>Epidermal</u> <u>hyperplasia</u> and <u>hyperpigmentation</u> (<u>acanthosis nigricans</u>)  [[3]](/library/eWYx4L)

* ↑ <u>Androgen</u> production in ovarian <u>theca interna</u> cells → imbalance between <u>androgen</u> precursors and the resulting <u>estrogen</u> produced in <u>granulosa cells</u>

* ↑ <u>LH</u> secretion disrupts the <u>LH</u>/<u>FSH</u> balance → impaired follicle maturation with cyst formation due to lack of follicle rupture → <u>anovulation</u>/oligoovulation → <u>infertility</u>

* ↑ <u>Androgen</u> precursor release and ↑ <u>estrogen</u> production in <u>adipose tissue</u>

* Inhibition of <u>SHBG</u> in the <u>liver</u> → ↑ free <u>androgens</u> and <u>estrogens</u> ;  [[4]](/library/sQXtxB)
* During <u>anovulatory cycles</u>, the lack of <u>progesterone</u> leads to increased unopposed <u>estrogen</u> exposure → <u>endometrial hyperplasia</u> → ↑ risk of <u>endometrial carcinoma</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Hyperandrogenism</u> in women is most commonly caused by PCOS.




![Pathophysiology of polycystic ovary syndrome](media/j0dvm64ayzgznhih7ou38lvt.jpg)

Pathophysiology of polycystic ovary syndrome

## Clinical features

Onset of symptoms typically occurs during <u>adolescence</u>.




* Menstrual irregularities

* Primary or <u>secondary amenorrhea</u>

* <u>Oligomenorrhea</u>

* <u>Menorrhagia</u>

* <u>Infertility</u> or difficulties conceiving

* <u>Insulin resistance</u> and associated conditions

* <u>Metabolic syndrome</u> (especially <u>obesity</u>) → ↑ risk of <u>sleep apnea</u>

* <u>Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease</u>

* <u>Skin</u> conditions

* <u>Hirsutism</u>

* <u>Androgenic alopecia</u>

* <u>Acne vulgaris</u>

* Oily <u>skin</u>

* <u>Acanthosis nigricans</u>

* Psychiatric conditions

* <u>Depression</u>

* <u>Anxiety disorders</u>





> [!TIP]
> Voice change may occur in severe forms of PCOS. However, it typically suggests a different underlying cause of <u>hyperandrogenism</u>.

---

## Differential diagnoses

### Hyperandrogenism [[5]](/library/G7XBMz)




#### Overview




* Definition: a state of excess <u>androgen</u> levels that causes symptoms such as growth of facial <u>hair</u>, deepening of the voice, and male-pattern baldness

* For more information about physiological <u>causes of hyperandrogenism</u>, see “<u>Pregnancy</u>.”





| <u>Differential diagnosis of hyperandrogenism</u> in female individuals |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Incidence</u> | Onset | Characteristic finding |
| PCOS | <br>* Most common (75–80% of cases)<br><br> | <br>* Peripubertal<br><br> | <br>* Polycystic <u>ovaries</u> on <u>pelvic</u> <u>ultrasound</u><br><br> |
| <u>Nonclassic CAH</u> | <br>* Common<br><br> | <br>* Peripubertal<br><br> | <br>* ↑ 17-Hydroxyprogesterone<br><br> |

| <u>Hypothyroidism</u> | <br>* Any time<br><br> | <br>* ↑ <u>TSH</u><br><br> |  |

| <u>Androgen</u>-secreting <u>tumor</u> (e.g., <u>Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor</u>, <u>adrenal adenoma</u>) | <br>* Primarily affects women 30–40 years of age<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Adrenal adenoma</u>: ↑ <u>DHEA-S</u> (> 700 Âµg/dL), <u>adrenal</u> mass<br><br>* <u>Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor</u>: normal <u>DHEA-S</u> levels, ovarian mass<br><br><br> |  |

#### Clinical features of hyperandrogenism




* Virilization: the appearance of male <u>secondary sexual characteristics</u> in a female individual

* Hirsutism: excessive male pattern <u>hair</u> growth (e.g., chin, upper lip, mid-<u>sternum</u>, abdomen, back, buttocks)

* Male-pattern <u>hair</u> loss

* <u>Acne</u>

* Increased muscle mass

* Voice deepening

* Clitoromegaly

* Rapid onset of <u>virilization</u> is suggestive of <u>exogenous</u> <u>androgen</u> intake or <u>androgen</u>-secreting tumors

* Manifestations of the underlying condition





#### Diagnostics of hyperandrogenism




* Laboratory tests to identify hyperandrogenemia

* ↑ Serum total <u>testosterone</u>

* ↓ <u>SHBG</u>

* <u>Free androgen index</u>

* Investigate for the underlying cause.





#### Treatment




* Medication to suppress or block <u>androgen</u> and manage symptoms of <u>virilization</u>

* <u>OCP</u>

* Antiandrogen drugs (e.g., <u>spironolactone</u>, <u>finasteride</u>)

* Treat the underlying cause (e.g., <u>surgery</u> for <u>androgen</u>-secreting tumors).





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[6]](/library/CZcqda0)[[7]](/library/00ceea0)[[8]](/library/SScy_b0)




Early diagnosis is essential, as PCOS is associated with many conditions, including metabolic dysfunction and impaired <u>fertility</u>. It also has a significant impact on a woman's emotional well-being and quality of life.




* Suspect PCOS in women of reproductive age with features of <u>hyperandrogenism</u> and/or <u>ovulatory dysfunction</u>.

* Use the <u>Rotterdam criteria</u> to establish the <u>clinical diagnosis</u>.

* Obtain an initial diagnostic workup to exclude <u>pregnancy</u> and endocrine disorders (e.g., <u>thyroid</u> dysfunction, <u>hyperprolactinemia</u>, <u>nonclassical CAH</u>).

* Perform a detailed assessment to evaluate for comorbidities.

* Screen for metabolic disorders  regardless of <u>BMI</u>.





### Rotterdam criteria [[6]](/library/CZcqda0)[[7]](/library/00ceea0)[[9]](/library/7804L3)




PCOS is diagnosed in adults based on the presence of at least two of the following criteria, after other endocrinological conditions, e.g., <u>thyroid disease</u>, <u>hyperprolactinemia</u>, have been excluded.




* <u>Oligoovulation</u> and/or <u>anovulation</u>

* <u>Hyperandrogenism</u> (based on clinical features or <u>laboratory studies</u>): Examine patients for signs of <u>acne</u>, <u>alopecia</u>, and <u>hirsutism</u>; obtain <u>laboratory studies</u> as needed.  [[6]](/library/CZcqda0)

* Enlarged and/or polycystic <u>ovary</u> on <u>ultrasound</u>  

* Ovarian volume ≥ 10 mL

* AND/OR the presence of multiple cystic follicles measuring 2–9 mm (string-of-pearls appearance) in one or both <u>ovaries</u>  [[7]](/library/00ceea0)





> [!WARNING]
> Diagnosing PCOS in <u>adolescents</u> is complex because PCOS symptoms overlap with normal <u>pubertal changes</u>. For this reason, the 2015 Pediatric Endocrine Society consensus does not endorse the use of <u>ultrasound</u> in <u>adolescents</u> to evaluate PCOS. [[10]](/library/BZczda0)









### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[6]](/library/CZcqda0)[[7]](/library/00ceea0)[[9]](/library/7804L3)




* Confirm <u>hyperandrogenism</u>: Obtain in all women with <u>clinical features of PCOS</u>, even if features are minimal or unclear. ;  [[7]](/library/00ceea0)

* ↑ <u>Testosterone</u>: Use the calculated free <u>testosterone</u>, calculated bioavailable <u>testosterone</u>, or <u>free androgen index</u>. Direct free <u>testosterone</u> has poor <u>sensitivity</u>. [[7]](/library/00ceea0)

* ↑ <u>Androstenedione</u> and ↑ <u>dehydroepiandrosterone</u> sulfate: limited role in diagnosis of PCOS, but useful for ruling out other <u>causes of hyperandrogenism</u>  [[7]](/library/00ceea0)

* Rule out differential diagnoses: e.g., <u>pregnancy</u>, endocrine disorders

* All patients

* <u>TSH</u>

* <u>Prolactin</u>

* <u>17-hydroxyprogesterone</u>

* Patients with <u>amenorrhea</u>

* Serum or urine <u>hCG</u>

* Serum <u>LH</u>, <u>FSH</u>

* See “<u>Diagnostics for amenorrhea</u>” for details.

* Features of <u>hypercortisolism</u>: Consider measuring <u>cortisol</u> in 24-hour urine, <u>late-night salivary cortisol</u>, or a <u>dexamethasone suppression test</u> (see “Diagnostics” in “<u>Cushing syndrome</u>”).





> [!TIP]
> A clinical picture of <u>hyperandrogenism</u> fulfills a diagnostic criterion of PCOS, even if serum <u>androgen</u> levels are normal.




> [!TIP]
> An elevated <u>LH</u> (with <u>LH</u>:<u>FSH</u> <u>ratio</u> > 2:1) is a characteristic finding in most patients with PCOS but not necessary for diagnosis.




### <u>Ultrasound</u> [[7]](/library/00ceea0)




* Parameters: An experienced clinician should assess the ovarian volume and, when feasible, the number and volume of follicles.  [[7]](/library/00ceea0)

* Modalities

* Transvaginal (preferred; use if acceptable to patient): offers the best visualization of <u>ovarian follicles</u>

* Transabdominal: should focus on measuring ovarian volume





> [!TIP]
> Identification of cystic follicles is not mandatory to diagnose PCOS.




### Evaluate for comorbidities [[6]](/library/CZcqda0)[[7]](/library/00ceea0)[[9]](/library/7804L3)




Patients with PCOS are at risk of serious comorbidities, even at a young age. It is important to screen for these at the first visit and at regular intervals.




* Metabolic screening and monitoring

* Measure weight, height, and <u>waist circumference</u>; calculate <u>BMI</u>. Measure at baseline and repeat every 6–12 months.

* For patients with elevated <u>BMI</u>: Obtain a <u>fasting lipid profile</u> and screen for <u>symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea</u>.

* Check blood pressure: Obtain at baseline and then at least once a year; measure more frequently based on individual risk.

* Assess glycemic status : Obtain at baseline and repeat every 1–3 years, depending on individual risk.

* Mental health and quality of life: Screen for <u>anxiety</u>, <u>depression</u>, and <u>sexual dysfunction</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Women with PCOS are at least twice as likely to have <u>metabolic syndrome</u> as women without PCOS. [[6]](/library/CZcqda0)




> [!TIP]
> Women with PCOS are also at increased risk for <u>endometrial cancer</u>. Screening is not routinely recommended, but clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion and conduct a <u>transvaginal ultrasound</u> and/or <u>endometrial sampling</u> if there are suggestive features (e.g., thickened <u>endometrium</u>, abnormal <u>vaginal bleeding</u>). [[7]](/library/00ceea0)

## Treatment

### Approach [[6]](/library/CZcqda0)[[7]](/library/00ceea0)[[8]](/library/SScy_b0)[[9]](/library/7804L3)




* Recommendations for all patients

* Encourage exercise and healthy eating (e.g. caloric restriction), and consider behavioral strategies and modifications (e.g., setting goals, eating more slowly).  [[6]](/library/CZcqda0)[[7]](/library/00ceea0)

* Target <u>BMI</u> < 25 kg/m<sup>2</sup> (can reduce <u>estrone</u> production in the <u>adipose tissue</u>)

* Screen for comorbidities and provide specific treatment.

* Tailor additional therapeutic interventions based on: 

* Reproductive goals

* Comorbidities

* Individual <u>risk factors</u>





> [!TIP]
> Features associated with PCOS (e.g., <u>obesity</u>, <u>hyperandrogenism</u>, difficulties conceiving) can have a negative psychosocial impact. If symptoms of <u>anxiety</u> and/or <u>depression</u> are identified, further mental health assessment and a referral to a mental health professional should be offered to the patient.




### Patients not planning to conceive [[6]](/library/CZcqda0)[[7]](/library/00ceea0)[[8]](/library/SScy_b0)[[9]](/library/7804L3)




For patients who do not wish to conceive, the therapeutic goals are to control menstrual irregularities and <u>hyperandrogenism</u>, treat comorbidities, and improve quality of life.




* <u>Combined oral contraceptives</u> (<u>COCs</u>)  [[8]](/library/SScy_b0)

* Indication: first-line treatment for <u>hyperandrogenism</u> and/or <u>menstrual cycle abnormalities</u>

* Additional benefits

* ↓ <u>Endometrial hyperplasia</u> → ↓ risk of <u>endometrial carcinoma</u>  [[10]](/library/BZczda0)

* ↓ Menstrual bleeding

* ↓ <u>Acne</u>

* Treatment of <u>hirsutism</u> 
* <u>Antiandrogens</u> can be added if results are unsatisfactory after 6 months of <u>COCs</u> and cosmetic therapy (e.g., electrolysis, laser, <u>photoepilation</u>). [[7]](/library/00ceea0)[[10]](/library/BZczda0)

* <u>Metformin</u>: improves menstrual irregularities, metabolic outcomes, and weight (especially when combined with lifestyle modifications)

* Second-line treatment for menstrual irregularity in patients unable to take or tolerate <u>COCs</u> [[9]](/library/7804L3)

* May be added to <u>COCs</u> and lifestyle modification to improve metabolic outcomes

* <u>Antiandrogens</u>: controversial role  [[7]](/library/00ceea0)

* Examples: <u>spironolactone</u>, <u>finasteride</u>, <u>flutamide</u>

* Indications: can be considered for treatment of <u>hirsutism</u> and <u>androgen</u>-related <u>alopecia</u> in patients unable to take or tolerate <u>COCs</u>

* Additional recommendation: When using <u>antiandrogens</u> as an alternative to <u>COCs</u>, it is advisable to use other forms of <u>contraception</u>.

* Additional interventions: Other measures, like <u>antiobesity medications</u> or <u>bariatric surgery</u>, may be considered on a case-by-case basis.





### Patients planning to conceive [[6]](/library/CZcqda0)[[7]](/library/00ceea0)[[9]](/library/7804L3)




The goals of treatment for patients who wish to conceive are management of comorbidities (e.g., weight loss for <u>overweight or obese</u> patients) and <u>induction of ovulation</u>.




* <u>Letrozole</u> (<u>off-label</u>): first-line therapy for <u>ovulation induction</u> DOSAGE  [[6]](/library/CZcqda0)[[11]](/library/kacmka0); 

* Improves <u>pregnancy</u> and <u>live birth</u> rates in patients with anovulatory <u>infertility</u> with no other causes

* Mechanism of action: <u>aromatase</u> inhibition reduces <u>estrogen</u> production, stimulating <u>FSH</u> secretion and inducing <u>ovulation</u>

* <u>Clomiphene</u>: alternative to <u>letrozole</u> 

* May be preferred over <u>metformin</u> monotherapy in <u>obese</u> women with anovulatory <u>infertility</u>  [[7]](/library/00ceea0)

* Mechanism of action: inhibits <u>hypothalamic</u> <u>estrogen</u> <u>receptors</u> → disruption of the negative feedback mechanism governing <u>estrogen</u> production → ↑ pulsatile secretion of <u>GnRH</u> → ↑ <u>FSH</u> and <u>LH</u> → stimulation of <u>ovulation</u>

* <u>Exogenous</u> <u>gonadotropins</u>: The low-dose regimen is the second-line treatment for <u>ovulation induction</u>.

* Agents: <u>exogenous</u> <u>FSH</u> and <u>human menopausal gonadotropin</u>

* Indication: typically used if first-line therapies are unsuccessful; occasionally used as first-line if the drug and monitoring requirements are accessible  [[7]](/library/00ceea0)

* <u>Metformin</u>

* Can be used as second-line monotherapy for <u>fertility</u> treatment.  [[7]](/library/00ceea0)

* Combination with <u>clomiphene</u> may increase <u>pregnancy</u> rates, especially in <u>obese</u> women.

* First-line therapy for <u>insulin resistance</u> [[8]](/library/SScy_b0)

* Additional <u>fertility</u> interventions

* Laparoscopic ovarian drilling

* A <u>laparoscopic</u> procedure in which ovarian tissue is reduced with a laser beam or surgical needle to decrease its volume and <u>androgen</u> production

* This hormonal shift can induce <u>FSH</u> secretion and improve ovarian function in patients with polycystic <u>ovary</u> syndrome.

* Second-line treatment for <u>ovulation induction</u>; can be performed as a first-line treatment if other indications for <u>laparoscopy</u> exist

* <u>In vitro fertilization</u>: can be offered as third-line therapy

* <u>Bariatric surgery</u>: no evidence of benefit in the <u>treatment of infertility</u>

* Management of other PCOS manifestations [[8]](/library/SScy_b0)

* <u>Hirsutism</u>: Nonpharmacological therapy is first-line (e.g., electrolysis, light-based <u>hair</u> removal via laser or <u>photoepilation</u>)

* <u>Acne</u>: Consider topical therapies (e.g., <u>benzoyl peroxide</u>, topical <u>antibiotics</u>)

---

## Complications

* Cardiovascular disease

* <u>Type 2 diabetes mellitus</u>

* <u>Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease</u>

* <u>Sleep apnea</u>

* <u>Malignancy</u> (increased risk before <u>menopause</u>) [[12]](/library/QoXub_)

* <u>Endometrial cancer</u>

* <u>Kidney cancer</u>

* <u>Pregnancy loss</u>

* <u>Depression</u> and <u>anxiety disorders</u>




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
